metaData.originalTitle: 大多数 AI Agent 公司，活不到 2030 年？
metaData.title: Most AI Agent Companies Won't Survive Until 2030?
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: In a roundtable discussion, five top VCs stated bluntly that most AI Agent companies have only created curiosity rather than dependency, and won't survive until 2030; the key to survival is building customer dependency through irreplaceability, clear ROI, and workflow integration.
metaData.summary: This article is compiled from a roundtable discussion at the Singapore Agent Summit, where five VCs (Golden Gate Ventures, Openspace Capital, 59st Ventures, Monk's Hill Ventures, Accel) shared their core criteria for evaluating AI Agent startups. The article first points out that most companies remain at the "curious" demo stage and fail to create "dependency"—meaning no one notices when the Agent disappears. The investors emphasize that the true moat is the "data flywheel" (proprietary data + iterative optimization), rather than static data; surviving companies must make Agents irreplaceable (replacing employee tasks), have quantifiable ROI (key metrics drop significantly when the Agent is unavailable), and deeply integrate into customer workflows. Additionally, globalization should start from Day 1, using the PESTLE framework to select the first market and focusing on a single pain point to the extreme. The five VCs also provided their respective "startup first aid kit" keywords, such as globalization, speed, resilience, unique insights, and data flywheel. The article concludes with "sleeping under the customer's desk for two weeks," emphasizing that entrepreneurs must be extremely obsessed with customer pain points.

mainPoints.point: Most AI Agent companies only create curiosity rather than dependency, and won't survive until 2030.
mainPoints.explanation: Jim Lim pointed out that if no one notices when an Agent disappears, it is just a tool; only by creating "dependency"—where the customer's business process is interrupted—does it become mission-critical.

mainPoints.point: The true moat is the data flywheel, not static proprietary data.
mainPoints.explanation: Yiliang believes that simply having data is not enough; the key lies in whether input data can be used to optimize models, and user feedback can be turned back into new data, forming an iterative loop.

mainPoints.point: Agent companies that survive must possess three characteristics: irreplaceability, clear ROI, and workflow integration.
mainPoints.explanation: Manasi emphasized the ability to 100% replace employees and immediately demonstrate ROI; Jeffrey noted that once integrated into workflows, customers "can't leave"; Jim believes that replacing employees rather than just enhancing efficiency is the prerequisite for getting paid.

mainPoints.point: Globalization should start from Day 1, using PESTLE to select the first market.
mainPoints.explanation: Jeffrey urged entrepreneurs to go directly to the target market, as Singapore is too comfortable; Jim suggested using the Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Legal, and Environmental framework to evaluate markets and choose the right soil.

mainPoints.point: Entrepreneurs must focus extremely on a single pain point and avoid spreading themselves too thin.
mainPoints.explanation: Arun shared his own failure experience: fighting on three fronts in Singapore, Hong Kong, and India almost killed the company; only after refocusing did they return to the growth track.

keyQuotes: If you're just enhancing efficiency, people won't pay for it.
A demo is the cheapest competitive moat.
Data itself is a still photo; a data flywheel is a movie in playback.
Sleep under the customer's desk for two weeks.

relatedArticles.title: Harness Is Not the Goal, Knowledge Is the Moat — Knowledge Accumulation Practices of an AI Engineering Delivery Team
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Based on the engineering delivery practices of an AI Team, this article proposes that knowledge accumulation is more important than workflow orchestration, and systematically introduces a complete methodology encompassing a five-layer knowledge storage architecture, a three-level maturity system, and how workflows serve knowledge accumulation.

relatedArticles.title: Redefining Skill Development: A Step-by-Step Guide & One-Stop Development Assistant Launch
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article systematically introduces the concept of AI Agent Skill, including its directory structure, writing standards, release process, and cross-platform challenges. It also launches a one-stop Skill development assistant, skill-dev-aio, designed to free developers from tedious tool learning and allow them to focus on experience and judgment.

relatedArticles.title: Investing 10,000 RMB in AI: A Year of Tools, Practices, and Reflections
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: A systematic summary of a veteran developer's practical experience in the AI wave, covering everything from MAC toolchain optimization and Harness Engineering architectural constraints to building an Agent-driven automated learning loop.

relatedArticles.title: Don't Rush to Multi-Agent — First, See Which Pitfalls Are Real
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Five practitioners review Multi-Agent applications across multiple scenarios, covering applicable conditions, model routing strategies, and memory system design, pointing out that the core issue isn't whether the AI is smart, but whether the business has role conflicts and game-theoretic needs.

relatedArticles.title: Understanding Hermes in One Article: How the New Top-Tier Agent Self-Evolves from Experience
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of the core innovation of the Hermes Agent—the Skills closed-loop system—detailing its complete implementation mechanism, from experience extraction and knowledge storage to intelligent retrieval and self-improvement, along with its engineering trade-offs and security considerations.

relatedArticles.title: Understanding Harness Engineering: Finding the Shell That Keeps AI from Going Rogue—Insights from 14 Engineering Articles | Hao's Trend Talk
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides an in-depth analysis of "Harness Engineering," a core technology in the AI Agent field. It reveals how to compensate for model shortcomings through a three-layer management architecture and proposes the logic of "Compensation Surface Migration" that evolves with model capabilities.

relatedArticles.title: Why Silicon Valley Is Hyping Agents, While the Most Profitable Companies Are Obsessed with Workflows?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article reviews the real-world commercialization insights shared by five female entrepreneurs at the Agent Summit in Singapore, revealing a counterintuitive conclusion: the companies that are truly making money are not fixated on Agents, but are using Workflows to solve specific problems in real scenarios.

relatedArticles.title: The Most Surreal Scene in AI Going Global Has Emerged: Singaporeans Want to Enter China, While Chinese Are Eager to Go Overseas
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article documents a roundtable discussion on AI going global, where four founders debate the definition of 'true globalization,' market selection, and entry strategies. The core takeaway is that globalization is not about escaping one market, but about first dominating a single market.

relatedArticles.title: Decoding the Silicon Valley AI Triangle: Capital, Talent, and Technology Converge. What Path for the Average Person?
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Through an in-depth conversation with Nodesk.ai founder Song Jian, this article explores the Silicon Valley AI ecosystem, the real state of AI Coding, the opportunities and pitfalls of the FDE model, and the irreplaceable human qualities in the AI era: taste and judgment.

relatedArticles.title: 6 Million Registered One-Person Companies, Less Than 10% May Survive
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Through a roundtable dialogue with four entrepreneurs from different backgrounds, this article analyzes the real dividends and harsh thresholds of One-Person Companies (OPC) in the AI era: the leverage effect is significant, but only compound elites with deep industry experience and business judgment can harness it.
